title: The Elevator Schedule
description: Order elevator stops from visible rules in four puzzles, repair two broken schedules slot by slot, then name the rule a draft broke and find the single swap that fixes another.

sections.title: Build the route
sections.description: Order each lift's stops using every rule.

sections.title: Repair the schedule
sections.description: Fix broken schedules slot by slot.

sections.title: Replay the break
sections.description: Spot which rule failed.

questions.prompt: Order the lift's four stops from first to last.
questions.context: The lift visits Lobby, Mailroom, Lab and Roof once each. Lobby is first. Mailroom comes before Lab. Roof is last.
questions.explanation: Lobby opens and Roof closes, leaving Mailroom and Lab in the middle, where Mailroom must come first.

questions.prompt: Order all five stops of this lift's run.
questions.context: Stops: Garage, Cafe, Gym, Studio, Terrace, each once. Garage is first. Terrace is last. Cafe is before Gym. Gym is before Studio.
questions.explanation: Garage and Terrace fix the ends. The three middle stops are chained Cafe, Gym, Studio, so only one order works.

questions.prompt: Order the five stops for this office lift.
questions.context: Stops: Archive, Print Shop, Vault, Atrium, Sky Deck, each once. Atrium is first. Sky Deck is last. Vault is before Archive. Print Shop is after Archive.
questions.explanation: After Atrium opens and Sky Deck closes, the rules chain Vault, Archive, Print Shop in the middle.

questions.prompt: This lift only travels upward. List its stops from lowest to highest.
questions.context: Stops: Parking, Tailor, Florist, Bakery, Cinema. Bakery is above Florist. Tailor is below Florist. Cinema is above Bakery. Tailor is above Parking.
questions.explanation: Chaining the clues gives Parking below Tailor, Tailor below Florist, Florist below Bakery, and Bakery below Cinema.

questions.prompt: Repair the schedule: choose the correct stop for each open slot.
questions.context: Rules: Dock is first, Roof is last, Library comes before Office, and Gym is immediately after Office. Broken draft: Dock, Office, Library, Gym, Roof. Slots 1 and 5 are already correct.
questions.explanation: Gym must directly follow Office, and Library must precede Office, so the middle must read Library, Office, Gym.

questions.prompt: Fix this second broken schedule by filling slots 2, 3 and 4.
questions.context: Rules: Parking is first, Observatory is last, Studio comes before Kitchen, and Library is immediately before Observatory. Broken draft: Parking, Library, Kitchen, Studio, Observatory.
questions.explanation: Library must sit right before Observatory in slot 4. That leaves Studio then Kitchen in slots 2 and 3.

questions.prompt: A draft for the first puzzle read Lobby, Lab, Mailroom, Roof. Which rule did it break?
questions.context: The first puzzle's rules: Lobby is first, Mailroom comes before Lab, and Roof is last. Each stop appears once.
questions.explanation: Lobby is first and Roof is last in the draft, but Lab appears before Mailroom, reversing the required pair.

questions.prompt: Which single swap of two stops repairs this draft: Dock, Library, Gym, Office, Roof?
questions.context: Rules: Dock is first, Roof is last, Library comes before Office, and Gym is immediately after Office.
questions.explanation: Swapping Gym and Office gives Dock, Library, Office, Gym, Roof. The other swaps move Dock or Roof, or leave Gym away from Office.

title: One Rule Is Wrong
description: Eight small rule puzzles: spot the one false rule in five rule sets, pick the rule whose removal leaves exactly one solution in two more, then rebuild a finishing order while ignoring a known false rule.

questions.prompt: Exactly one rule is false. Which rule must go to make the rest consistent?
questions.context: Four items A, B, C, D are placed in a line. Rule 1: A precedes B. Rule 2: B precedes C. Rule 3: A precedes C. Rule 4: C precedes A. Rule 5: D is last.
questions.explanation: Rules 1 and 2 force A, B, C in that order, and Rule 3 agrees. Rule 4 reverses it. Dropping Rule 4 leaves only A, B, C, D.

questions.prompt: Exactly one of these rules about whole numbers x, y, z is false. Which one?
questions.context: Rule 1: x + y = 10. Rule 2: x is less than y. Rule 3: y + z = 12. Rule 4: x + z = 14. Rule 5: y is the smallest of the three.
questions.explanation: Adding Rules 1, 3 and 4 gives 2(x + y + z) = 36, so x + y + z = 18 and x = 6, y = 4, z = 8. Rule 5 holds but Rule 2 fails. Dropping any other rule leaves Rule 2 clashing with Rule 5 or with the sums.

options.label: Rule 2: x is less than y

questions.prompt: A token is hidden in one of boxes 1 to 4. Exactly one rule is false. Which?
questions.context: Rule 1: it is in box 3 or 4. Rule 2: it is in an even-numbered box. Rule 3: it is in box 1 or 2. Rule 4: it is not in box 1. Rule 5: it is not in box 4.
questions.explanation: Boxes 1, 3 and 4 each make at least two rules false. Only box 2 makes just one rule false, and that rule is Rule 1.

questions.prompt: One rule in this invented conference schedule is false. Which rule creates the impossible loop?
questions.context: Speakers Xan, Yara and Zed take slots 1, 2 and 3, one per slot. Rule 1: Yara is in slot 2. Rule 2: Zed is before Yara. Rule 3: Yara is before Xan. Rule 4: Xan is not in slot 1. Rule 5: Xan is before Zed.
questions.explanation: Rules 2, 3 and 5 form a loop: Zed, Yara, Xan, Zed. Removing Rule 5 gives Zed, Yara, Xan, which also satisfies Rules 1 and 4.

questions.prompt: Exactly one rule about the mystery number N is false. Which rule?
questions.context: N is a two-digit whole number. Rule 1: N is a multiple of 7. Rule 2: N is between 40 and 60. Rule 3: its digits add to 13. Rule 4: N is even. Rule 5: N is a perfect square.
questions.explanation: Rules 1, 2, 3 and 5 all point to 49, which is odd. Removing any other rule leaves no number that satisfies the rest.

questions.prompt: No seating satisfies all four rules. Which removal leaves exactly one valid seating?
questions.context: Ana, Ben, Cal and Dev take seats 1 to 4, one each. Rule 1: Cal is in seat 4. Rule 2: Dev is not in seat 1. Rule 3: Ben is in seat 1. Rule 4: Ana sits directly left of Ben, in the next lower seat.
questions.explanation: Rules 3 and 4 clash. Removing Rule 4 leaves two seatings. Removing Rule 3 leaves only Ana, Ben, Dev, Cal in seats 1 to 4.

questions.prompt: No whole number from 1 to 12 satisfies all five rules. Removing which rule leaves exactly one?
questions.context: Rule 1: N is even. Rule 2: N is greater than 3. Rule 3: N is a multiple of 5. Rule 4: N is less than 9. Rule 5: N is not 5.
questions.explanation: Even multiples of 5 are only 10, which breaks Rule 4. Removing Rule 4 leaves exactly 10, while removing Rule 3 leaves 4, 6 and 8.

questions.prompt: Rule 3 is the known false rule. Ignore it and arrange the runners from first to last.
questions.context: Race results for five invented runners. Rule 1: Rae finished first. Rule 2: Pia finished directly after Omar. Rule 3: Pia finished before Ines. Rule 4: Quin finished last. Rule 5: Ines finished before Omar.
questions.explanation: Rae is first and Quin last, leaving three middle places. Ines before Omar, with Pia directly after Omar, forces Ines, Omar, Pia.

title: A Message With Missing Punctuation
description: Eight texts arrive with their punctuation stripped. Use the stated facts to choose the punctuation that makes exactly one reading possible, then solve two messages that must satisfy two facts at once.

questions.prompt: Which punctuation of the text fits the fact below without changing any words?
questions.context: Text: Call the cook Sam. Fact: Sam is the person being asked to phone the cook.
questions.explanation: A comma before Sam marks direct address, so Sam is told to call the cook. Without it, Sam could be the cook's name.

questions.prompt: Which punctuation of the text matches the stated fact?
questions.context: Text: I saw a man eating shark. Fact: the message reports a dangerous animal that preys on people.
questions.explanation: The hyphen in man-eating joins the words into one adjective describing the shark. The other versions describe a person eating shark.

options.label: I saw a man eating shark.
I saw a man, eating shark.
I saw, a man eating shark.

questions.prompt: Match each punctuated text to the person it says is running late.
questions.context: Each text uses only commas to separate the speaker from the spoken words. Two of the texts report the same person as late.
questions.explanation: Commas around said mark the speaker. In the first text Lee speaks about Mia; in the second Mia speaks about Lee; in the third Mia speaks about Lee again.

questions.prompt: Which version fits the stated fact about this text?
questions.context: Text: Most of the time travelers worry. Fact: the message is about worried people who travel through time.
questions.explanation: Time travelers is one noun phrase, so no comma may split it. Adding a comma or period after time turns it into an adverb meaning usually.

options.label: Most of the time, travelers worry.
Most of the time travelers worry.
Most of the time. Travelers worry.
Most of the time: travelers worry.

questions.prompt: Which punctuation of the text fits the fact?
questions.context: Text: My brother who lives in Perth is visiting. Fact: the writer has three brothers and is singling out the one in Perth.
questions.explanation: The clause who lives in Perth is needed to identify which brother, so it takes no commas. Commas would suggest the writer has only one brother.

options.label: My brother, who lives in Perth, is visiting.
My brother who lives in Perth is visiting.
My brother who lives, in Perth is visiting.
My brother who lives in Perth, is visiting.

questions.prompt: Which punctuation of the text fits the stated fact?
questions.context: Text: While Eli cooked Ana watched. Fact: Ana is a person watching, and nobody is being cooked.
questions.explanation: The comma after cooked ends the opening clause, so Eli cooked and Ana watched. Placing it after Ana makes her the thing cooked.

questions.prompt: Which single version satisfies both facts about this text?
questions.context: Text: We hired the cooks Nia and Omar and Pat. Fact 1: Nia and Omar are the cooks. Fact 2: Pat is a third hire who is not one of the cooks.
questions.explanation: Commas around Nia and Omar make them the cooks, and the final comma and Pat adds a separate hire. The other versions make Pat a cook.

options.label: We hired the cooks, Nia, Omar, and Pat.
We hired the cooks, Nia and Omar, and Pat.
We hired the cooks Nia, Omar, and Pat.
We hired the cooks, Nia and Omar and Pat.

questions.prompt: For each text, pick the one version that satisfies both of its facts.
questions.explanation: Hyphens group five-year-old as one unit, leaving twenty as the count. An apostrophe before the s shows one team owns several captains.

cells.label: We planted twenty five year old trees. Facts: there were twenty trees, and each tree was five years old.
My teams captains cheered. Facts: the writer belongs to exactly one team, and that team has more than one captain.

title: The Two-Way Clue
description: Solve eight crossword-style clues where a definition and a letter rule must both fit. Pick the single matching word, match clues to answers, and spot decoys that satisfy only one half.

sections.title: Fit Both Halves
sections.description: Find the one word that satisfies the definition and the letter rule.

sections.title: Spot the Decoy
sections.description: Identify which half of the clue a decoy fails.

questions.prompt: Which listed word satisfies both the definition and the letter rule?
questions.context: Definition: a place to borrow books. Letter rule: seven letters, second letter I.
questions.explanation: LIBRARY has seven letters, I is second, and you borrow books there. LIBRARIES is nine letters, LITERAL is not a place, and BOOKING has O second.

questions.prompt: Which word fits both the meaning and every letter requirement?
questions.context: Definition: a very large body of salt water. Letter rule: five letters, starts with O, ends with N.
questions.explanation: OCEAN meets all three letter requirements and names a vast salt-water body. ORGAN fits only the letters, while GULF and ORBIT fail the letter rule.

questions.prompt: Which option satisfies both halves of this clue?
questions.context: Definition: a yellow citrus fruit. Letter rule: five letters, starts with LE.
questions.explanation: LEMON is a yellow citrus fruit with five letters beginning LE. LEMUR matches only the letters, while CITRON matches only the definition at six letters.

questions.prompt: Pick the only word that meets the definition and the letter rule.
questions.context: Definition: a glazed opening in a wall. Letter rule: six letters, second letter I, last letter W.
questions.explanation: WINDOW is glazed, sits in a wall, and fits W-I-N-D-O-W. WILLOW matches the letters only, while SKYLIGHT and DOORWAY break both the rule and the meaning.

questions.prompt: Match each two-part clue to the one word that satisfies both halves.
questions.context: One answer word is a decoy and will be left unused.
questions.explanation: NEST, STORM and HONEY each satisfy their definition and their letters. MONEY ends in Y with five letters, but it is not made by bees.

left.label: Where a bird lays eggs; four letters, second letter E
Heavy rain with thunder; five letters, starts with S
Sweet spread made by bees; five letters, ends in Y

questions.prompt: For each clue, choose the word satisfying both the definition and letter rule.
questions.explanation: OCTOPUS beats OCTOBER on meaning, PIANO beats PATIO and CELLO on keys and ending, and SLOW is the only S-word that is the opposite of fast.

cells.label: Eight-armed sea creature; seven letters, starts with O
Instrument with black and white keys; five letters, ends in O
Opposite of fast; four letters, starts with S

questions.prompt: Which option fits the definition but breaks the letter rule?
questions.context: Definition: an insect that makes honey. Letter rule: three letters, starts with B.
questions.explanation: HONEYBEE describes an insect that makes honey, but it has eight letters. BEE fits both halves, while BUG and BED fit only the letters.

questions.prompt: Which option fits the letter rule but not the definition?
questions.context: Definition: the body part used for seeing. Letter rule: three letters, ends in E.
questions.explanation: AXE has three letters ending in E, but it is a tool, not a body part. EYE fits both halves, while SIGHT and EAR break the letter rule.

title: The Helpful Red Herring
description: Eight mini-mysteries. First spot the one clue you can safely ignore in five cases, then solve three more using only the clues that matter.

sections.title: Spot the herring
sections.description: Each case has exactly one clue you can remove without changing the answer.

sections.title: Solve without it
sections.description: The herring is named. Use the remaining clues to crack the case.

questions.prompt: Which clue can be ignored while still pinning down the locker?
questions.context: A bag is in one of lockers 1, 2, 3 or 4. Clue 1: it is not in locker 1. Clue 2: it is not in locker 2. Clue 3: it is not in locker 4. Clue 4: its owner likes red.
questions.explanation: Clues 1, 2 and 3 remove lockers 1, 2 and 4, leaving locker 3. A favorite color says nothing about where the bag is.

questions.prompt: Which clue is unnecessary for identifying the umbrella's owner?
questions.context: An umbrella belongs to exactly one of Mira, Jun, Tala or Omar. Clue 1: Mira, Jun or Tala. Clue 2: Jun, Tala or Omar. Clue 3: not Tala. Clue 4: the handle is yellow.
questions.explanation: Clues 1 and 2 together leave Jun or Tala, and clue 3 removes Tala. Drop any of those three and two owners remain; the handle color never narrows the names.

questions.prompt: Which clue adds nothing to the search for the secret number?
questions.context: A secret whole number is between 10 and 30 inclusive. Clue 1: it is a multiple of 7. Clue 2: it is greater than 15. Clue 3: it is even. Clue 4: it has two digits.
questions.explanation: Multiples of 7 in range are 14, 21 and 28. Greater than 15 drops 14, and even drops 21, leaving 28. Every number from 10 to 30 already has two digits.

questions.prompt: Four runners finished a race with no ties. Which clue is irrelevant to finding the winner?
questions.context: Runners: Kai, Lena, Mo, Nia. Clue 1: Kai finished ahead of Lena. Clue 2: Lena finished ahead of Mo. Clue 3: Mo finished ahead of Nia. Clue 4: Nia wore a green bib.
questions.explanation: Clues 1 to 3 form a chain Kai, Lena, Mo, Nia, so Kai won. Remove any one of them and another runner could be first. The bib color changes no positions.

options.label: Clue 4: Nia wore a green bib

questions.prompt: Which clue can be dropped and still leave exactly one key holder?
questions.context: Candidates: Priya, Quinn, Rosa, Sam, Tess. Priya, Rosa and Sam wear glasses; Quinn and Tess do not. Clue 1: the holder wears glasses. Clue 2: not Priya. Clue 3: not Sam. Clue 4: the holder arrived by bus.
questions.explanation: Glasses leave Priya, Rosa and Sam; excluding Priya and Sam leaves Rosa. Without any of clues 1 to 3 a second candidate remains. Bus travel is never linked to anyone.

questions.prompt: Arrange the band members in the order they walk on stage, first to last.
questions.context: Clue 1: Jo walks on before Ivy. Clue 2: Ivy walks on before Lu. Clue 3: Lu walks on before Kit. Clue 4 is the herring: Kit's jacket is orange. Use clues 1 to 3 only.
questions.explanation: The three precedence clues chain together as Jo, then Ivy, then Lu, then Kit. The jacket color gives no information about the order.

questions.prompt: Match each student to their pet using only clues 1 and 2.
questions.context: Ana, Ben and Cho each own a different pet: a cat, a dog or a fish. In this case the cat and dog have fur, the fish has none, and only the dog barks. Clue 1: Ana's pet has no fur. Clue 2: Ben's pet barks. Clue 3 is the herring: Cho's backpack is green.
questions.explanation: Only the fish lacks fur, so Ana owns the fish. Only the dog barks, so Ben owns the dog. That leaves the cat for Cho.

questions.prompt: Ignoring the herring, who returned the library book?
questions.context: Exactly one of Dara, Eli, Fay or Gus returned it. Clue 1: not Dara. Clue 2: not Gus. Clue 3: Eli was away in another city all week. Clue 4 is the herring: the book has a blue cover.
questions.explanation: Clues 1 and 2 remove Dara and Gus, and clue 3 removes Eli, who was away. Fay is the only one left; the cover color is irrelevant.

title: The Three-Layer Alibi
description: Solve grid and matching puzzles that link suspects to times, times to places, and places to witnesses, then spot the one alibi that cracks.

questions.prompt: Assign each suspect to the time they signed the archive visitor log.
questions.context: Invented case. Four suspects each signed at a different time: 9:00 am, 10:30 am, 12:00 noon or 2:00 pm. Mara signed before Inés. Kofi signed last. Theo signed in the slot immediately after Inés.
questions.explanation: Kofi takes 2:00 pm. Mara must precede Inés, and Theo directly follows Inés, so the order is Mara, Inés, Theo, then Kofi.

questions.prompt: A second badge printer logged four sign-ins. Assign each person to their time.
questions.context: Invented case. Times are 8:00, 9:30, 11:00 and 12:30, one per person. Lucía signed in exactly three hours after Amara. Hiro signed last. Jonas did not sign first.
questions.explanation: Hiro takes 12:30, so Lucía cannot be three hours after a 9:30 start. Amara is 8:00, Lucía 11:00, and Jonas gets 9:30.

questions.prompt: Match each time slot to the place where it happened. Places can be used more than once.
questions.context: Invented case. Only the Archive and the Café hosted slots; none took place at the Dock. The 9:00 and 12:00 slots shared a place, and the 10:30 and 2:00 slots shared the other. A coffee-machine receipt printed at 10:30.
questions.explanation: The coffee receipt puts 10:30 in the Café, so 2:00 joins it there. The other pair, 9:00 and 12:00, must be the Archive. The Dock stays unused.

questions.prompt: Assign each of four consecutive slots to the room where it took place.
questions.context: Invented case. Slots run first to fourth. The first slot was in the Workshop. The Archive hosted exactly two slots, with one slot between them. The Garden slot came directly after the first Archive slot. Every room option is used at most once except the Archive.
questions.explanation: The Archive pair with a gap, after a Workshop start, must be slots two and four. The Garden directly follows slot two, so it is slot three.

questions.prompt: Match each witness to the place they watched from. Several witnesses can share a place.
questions.context: Invented case. Ana and Ben watched from the same place. Chi was at the Café. Ana was not at the Café. Dev was not with Chi or with Ana. The Dock had exactly one witness.
questions.explanation: Ana and Ben cannot share the Dock, since it has one witness, so they are at the Archive. Dev avoids the Café and the Archive, leaving the Dock.

questions.prompt: Place each witness at the location where they were stationed.
questions.context: Invented case. Nobody was at the Dock or on the Roof. Priya was not in the Archive. Lena was in the same place as Priya. Omar was alone.
questions.explanation: Only the Archive and Café are in use. Priya must be in the Café, Lena joins her, and Omar, being alone, takes the Archive.

questions.prompt: Check all three layers. Which suspect's alibi is the one that cracks?
questions.context: Invented case. Verified places: 9:00 and 12:00 were at the Archive; 10:30 and 2:00 were at the Café. Witnesses: Ana and Ben at the Archive, Chi at the Café, Dev at the Dock. Claims: Mara, 9:00, Archive, Ana. Inés, 10:30, Café, Chi. Theo, 12:00, Archive, Ben. Kofi, 2:00, Dock, Dev.
questions.explanation: Mara, Inés and Theo each name the verified place for their time, with a witness there. Kofi claims the Dock at 2:00, but the verified place was the Café.

questions.prompt: Using the same case, who could genuinely have seen whoever was at the verified 2:00 place?
questions.context: Same invented case: the verified 2:00 place was the Café. Ana and Ben watched the Archive, Chi watched the Café, and Dev watched the Dock.
questions.explanation: The verified 2:00 slot was in the Café, and Chi is the only witness stationed there. Ana and Ben saw the Archive, while Dev saw the Dock.

title: The Museum Label Mix-Up
description: Reassign fallen labels in an invented museum by using size, weight, age, noise and room-order hints, including cases that share several labels.

questions.prompt: Match each fallen label to the case where it belongs. Cases can hold several labels.
questions.context: Invented exhibits and lengths: Glass Bead 2 cm, Moon-dial 4 cm, Copper Comb 7 cm, Clay Lamp 9 cm, Tin Whistle 12 cm, Reed Boat 30 cm. Case A holds the two smallest items. Case C holds only the longest item. Case B holds the rest.
questions.explanation: The two shortest items, Bead and Moon-dial, go to Case A. The Reed Boat is alone in Case C. Comb, Lamp and Whistle are left for Case B.

questions.prompt: Use the weight hints to assign each label to its case.
questions.context: Invented exhibits: Stone Mortar 8 kg, Wood Drum 3 kg, Iron Key Ring 1 kg, Felt Hat 1 kg, Clay Jug 3 kg. Case 1 holds items lighter than the Drum. Case 2 holds items weighing the same as the Drum. Case 3 holds the heaviest item.
questions.explanation: Key Ring and Hat are lighter than 3 kg, so Case 1. Drum and Jug both weigh 3 kg, so Case 2. The Mortar is heaviest, so Case 3.

questions.prompt: Place each label in the right room's case, using the noise and size hints.
questions.context: Invented rooms in a line, one case each. Noise: Room 1 is 40 dB, Room 2 is 55 dB, Room 3 is 35 dB. Labels: Pearl Button 2 cm, Cedar Flute 14 cm, Rope Ladder 40 cm. The longest label sits in a room beside the quietest room. The Flute's room is louder than the Button's room.
questions.explanation: Room 3 is quietest, and its only neighbor is Room 2, so the Ladder goes there. The Flute's room must be louder than the Button's, so Flute in Room 1, Button in Room 3.

questions.prompt: Arrange the five invented rooms in tour order, first to last, using every hint.
questions.context: Hints: Lantern Room comes after Kite Room. Salt Room comes after Clock Room. Kite Room comes after Salt Room. Loom Room comes before Clock Room.
questions.explanation: Chaining the hints gives Loom, Clock, Salt, Kite, Lantern. Each hint links neighbors, so together they leave only one possible tour order.

questions.prompt: Exactly two labels were swapped. Which pair must be swapped back?
questions.context: Invented tour, rooms 1 to 4 in order, one case each. Posted now: Room 1 Brass Gear, Room 2 Wool Sash, Room 3 Paper Kite, Room 4 Salt Bowl. Hints: the Sash is in an earlier room than the Gear. The Bowl is in the last room. The Kite is exactly one room before the Bowl. The Gear is in Room 2.
questions.explanation: Bowl in Room 4, Kite in 3 and Gear in 2 are fixed by the hints, leaving the Sash in Room 1. So Gear and Sash were swapped.

questions.prompt: Assign each label to a room using the age-gap hints relative to the Mask.
questions.context: Invented ages: Lamp 900 years, Comb 850, Mask 600, Bell 580, Spindle 300. Amber Room holds items at least 200 years older than the Mask. Cedar Room holds items at least 250 years younger than the Mask. Birch Room holds everything else, including the Mask.
questions.explanation: Amber needs 800 years or more: Lamp and Comb. Cedar needs 350 or less: only Spindle. Mask and Bell fall in between, so they go to Birch.

questions.prompt: Three labels are 3, 6 and 9 cm. Case A holds two, including the 3 cm label. Which added clue makes the placement unique?
questions.context: Case B holds the remaining label. So far the second label in Case A could be either the 6 cm or the 9 cm one.
questions.explanation: Only 3 + 6 equals 9 cm, so that clue fixes Case A as the 3 and 6 labels. The other clues fit both possibilities or repeat what is known.

options.label: Case B's label is longer than 5 cm
Case A's two labels total 9 cm
Case A contains the smallest label
Case B's label is not 3 cm

questions.prompt: Solve the final room map: place each invented label in its case.
questions.context: Rooms in a line: Room 1 holds Case A (50 dB), Room 2 holds Case B (30 dB), Room 3 holds Case C (45 dB). Labels: Pin 3 cm, Needle 6 cm, Spoon 11 cm, Ladle 25 cm. Case A holds exactly the two smallest items and nothing else. The longest label sits in a case beside the quietest room's case. Case B holds exactly one item.
questions.explanation: Pin and Needle fill Case A. Room 2 is quietest, so the Ladle must be in a neighboring case; A is full, so it goes to Case C. The Spoon is the one item for Case B.

title: Repair the Transit Diagram
description: Study tiny invented metro maps, tap the link that breaks the stated rules, repair two-link errors, then count rides on corrected maps.

sections.title: Find the wrong link
sections.description: Each map has exactly one link that breaks its rules.

sections.title: Two-link repairs
sections.description: Two links are wrong; choose the pair to remove.

questions.prompt: Which direct link violates the route requirement?
questions.context: Invented stations: Pine, Mill, Quay, Dock. Links: Pine–Mill, Mill–Quay, Mill–Dock, Pine–Quay. Rule: the shortest Pine-to-Quay trip must take exactly two links, passing through Mill.
questions.explanation: Pine–Quay lets riders go directly in one link. Removing it leaves Pine–Mill–Quay as the shortest trip, while the other three links are still needed.

diagram.title: Link list for Pine, Mill, Quay and Dock
diagram.description: Schematic only, not geographic. Each rectangle is one link on the map: top row Pine–Mill and Mill–Quay, bottom row Mill–Dock and Pine–Quay.

questions.prompt: Tap the one link that makes the stated trip length impossible.
questions.context: Invented stations: Ash, Birch, Cedar, Delta. Links: Ash–Birch, Birch–Cedar, Cedar–Delta, Ash–Cedar. Rules: every station stays connected, and the shortest Ash-to-Delta trip takes exactly three links.
questions.explanation: Ash–Cedar creates the two-link trip Ash–Cedar–Delta. Without it, the only route is Ash–Birch–Cedar–Delta, which is three links, and every station stays connected.

diagram.title: Link list for Ash, Birch, Cedar and Delta
diagram.description: Schematic only, not geographic. Each rectangle is one link: top row Ash–Cedar and Ash–Birch, bottom row Birch–Cedar and Cedar–Delta.

questions.prompt: Which link breaks the interchange rule?
questions.context: Invented stations: Central, Fern, Gate, Holt. Links: Central–Fern, Fern–Gate, Central–Gate, Central–Holt. Rule: Fern, Gate and Holt may reach one another only by passing through Central.
questions.explanation: Fern–Gate lets riders travel between those two stations without Central. The other three links each connect an outer station to Central, which the rule requires.

diagram.title: Link list for the Central interchange
diagram.description: Schematic only, not geographic. Each rectangle is one link: top row Central–Fern and Fern–Gate, bottom row Central–Gate and Central–Holt.

questions.prompt: Which link must go so the map becomes a single line with the required ends?
questions.context: Invented stations: Reed, Sand, Tide, Vale. Links: Reed–Sand, Sand–Tide, Sand–Vale, Tide–Vale. Rules: no station has more than two links, all stations stay connected, and the line's two ends are Reed and Vale.
questions.explanation: Sand has three links, so one must go. Removing Sand–Vale gives Reed–Sand–Tide–Vale, ending at Reed and Vale. Removing Sand–Tide would make Tide an end instead.

diagram.title: Link list for Reed, Sand, Tide and Vale
diagram.description: Schematic only, not geographic. Each rectangle is one link: top row Reed–Sand and Sand–Tide, bottom row Sand–Vale and Tide–Vale.

questions.prompt: Which pair of links should be removed to satisfy both rules?
questions.context: Invented stations: Quill, Rook, Sage, Thorn, Umber. Links: Quill–Rook, Rook–Sage, Sage–Thorn, Thorn–Umber, Quill–Sage, Rook–Umber. Rules: the shortest Quill-to-Thorn trip takes exactly three links, and Umber's only link is to Thorn.
questions.explanation: Quill–Sage shortcuts the trip to two links, and Rook–Umber gives Umber a second connection. Removing both leaves Quill–Rook–Sage–Thorn–Umber, which meets both rules.

questions.prompt: Which two links should be removed so every rule holds?
questions.context: Invented stations: Ivy, Jade, Kite, Lime, Moor. Links: Ivy–Jade, Jade–Kite, Kite–Lime, Lime–Moor, Ivy–Kite, Jade–Lime. Rules: no three stations all link to each other, Ivy links only to Jade, and the shortest Ivy-to-Moor trip is four links.
questions.explanation: Ivy–Kite must go because Ivy links only to Jade. Jade–Lime must also go to break the Jade–Kite–Lime triangle while keeping the Ivy-to-Moor trip at four links.

questions.prompt: On this repaired map, how many links does each shortest trip use?
questions.context: Repaired invented map with stations Dune, Eel, Fog, Glen, Hush, Isle. Links: Dune–Eel, Eel–Fog, Fog–Glen, Fog–Hush, Hush–Isle. Count the fewest links for each trip.
questions.explanation: Dune to Glen runs Dune–Eel–Fog–Glen. Eel to Isle runs Eel–Fog–Hush–Isle. Glen to Hush runs Glen–Fog–Hush. Dune to Isle takes Dune–Eel–Fog–Hush–Isle.

questions.prompt: Tap the one link whose removal would cut a station off from the rest.
questions.context: Invented stations: Cliff, Dale, Echo, Fjord. Links: Cliff–Dale, Dale–Echo, Echo–Cliff, Echo–Fjord.
questions.explanation: Cliff, Dale and Echo form a loop, so any one of those links can close and riders still get around. Echo–Fjord is Fjord's only connection.

diagram.title: Link list for Cliff, Dale, Echo and Fjord
diagram.description: Schematic only, not geographic. Each rectangle is one link: top row Cliff–Dale and Echo–Fjord, bottom row Dale–Echo and Echo–Cliff.
