note: All stations, links and rules are invented for this quiz and do not depict any real transit system. Each map is given as a text list of links, shown as tappable rectangles.

title: The Awkward Seating Chart
description: Place invented guests in a straight row using explicit adjacency rules, then repair seating charts that break a rule.

questions.prompt: Arrange the guests from seat 1 (left) to seat 5 (right).
questions.context: Rules: Lee is in the first seat. Mo is in the last seat. Kim, Pat and Jo sit in consecutive seats, in that left-to-right order.
questions.explanation: Lee and Mo fill the two ends, which leaves seats 2 to 4 for Kim, Pat and Jo in their stated order.

questions.prompt: Who sits in seat 4 of the five-seat row?
questions.context: Seats run 1 to 5 from left to right. Dee sits in seat 1. Eli sits directly right of Dee. Fay sits directly left of Gus. Hal does not sit in seat 5.
questions.explanation: Dee is in seat 1 and Eli in seat 2. Fay-Gus can only fit in seats 3-4 or 4-5; Hal cannot be in seat 5, so Hal takes seat 3, Fay seat 4, Gus seat 5.

questions.prompt: Fill in who sits in each seat of the four-seat row.
questions.context: Rules: Nia sits directly right of Omar. Priya sits in an end seat. Quinn is not next to Priya. Quinn sits somewhere left of Omar.
questions.explanation: The Omar-Nia pair can only work in seats 2-3: seats 1-2 or 3-4 would force Priya and Quinn together. Quinn must be left of Omar, so Quinn is in seat 1 and Priya in seat 4.

questions.prompt: Match each guest to their seat in the five-seat row.
questions.context: Rules: Dev sits in seat 1. Ana sits left of Ben with exactly one seat between them. Esi sits in that middle seat. Chloe sits in an end seat.
questions.explanation: Ana, Esi and Ben form a block of three. With Dev in seat 1, the block fits seats 2-4, leaving the end seat 5 for Chloe.

questions.prompt: How many different seating charts satisfy every rule?
questions.context: Five seats in a row. Ivy is first and Zed is last. Ola, Raj and Sue fill the middle three seats in some order. Ola and Sue must not sit next to each other.
questions.explanation: Ola and Sue are only non-adjacent in the middle block if they take seats 2 and 4, leaving Raj in seat 3. They can swap sides, giving exactly 2 charts.

questions.prompt: Exactly one rule below is broken by the chart. Which one?
questions.context: Current chart, seats 1 to 5: Tia, Uma, Vic, Wes, Xan. Rules: Tia is in seat 1. Uma sits next to Vic. Wes is not next to Xan. Uma is not in seat 3. Xan sits in an end seat.

options.label: Wes is not next to Xan
Xan sits in an end seat

questions.explanation: Wes is in seat 4 and Xan in seat 5, so they are adjacent. Every other listed rule is satisfied by this chart.

questions.prompt: Which single swap of two guests repairs the chart without breaking any other rule?
questions.context: Chart, seats 1 to 5: Tia, Uma, Vic, Wes, Xan. Rules: Tia is in seat 1. Uma sits next to Vic. Wes is not next to Xan. Uma is not in seat 3. Xan sits in an end seat.
questions.explanation: Swapping Wes and Uma gives Tia, Wes, Vic, Uma, Xan. Uma and Vic are adjacent, Wes and Xan are apart, and all other rules hold. The other swaps still break a rule.

questions.prompt: Repair this table: fill in the one valid chart for all four rules.
questions.context: Broken chart, seats 1 to 4: Gia, Hugo, Iris, Jon. Rules: Iris sits next to Jon. Gia is not in seat 1. Hugo sits somewhere left of Iris. Jon sits in an end seat.
questions.explanation: Jon in seat 1 would leave no room for Hugo to be left of Iris. So Jon is in seat 4, Iris in 3, and Gia must take seat 2, which leaves Hugo in seat 1.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All guest names and seating rules are invented for these puzzles; each puzzle supplies every rule you need.

title: Ask One Better Question
description: Compare yes/no questions by their worst-case leftover group, plan a search, then follow supplied answers through a short investigation to find a hidden item.

sections.title: Choose the split
sections.description: Compare questions by the largest group they could leave.

sections.title: Use what you know
sections.description: Adapt to earlier information and rank questions.

sections.title: Follow the answers
sections.description: Pick an investigation and isolate the hidden item.

questions.prompt: Which yes/no question leaves the fewest candidates in the worst case?
questions.context: Worst case means the larger group left after the answer. Traits (Plugs in / Heats / Has moving part / Kitchen item): Kettle Y,Y,N,Y. Lamp Y,N,N,N. Mug N,N,N,Y. Clock Y,N,Y,N. Radio Y,N,N,N. Fan Y,N,Y,N. Toaster Y,Y,N,Y. Blender Y,N,Y,Y.

options.label: Does it have a moving part?

questions.explanation: Kitchen splits the eight objects 4 and 4. Plugging in leaves up to 7, heating up to 6, and moving parts up to 5.

questions.prompt: For each question, choose the largest number of travelers that could remain after hearing the answer.
questions.context: Nine travelers carry items (Coat / Hat / Bag): Ana Y,Y,Y. Bo Y,N,Y. Cy Y,Y,N. Di N,Y,Y. Eli N,N,Y. Fay Y,N,N. Gus N,Y,N. Hana N,N,N. Ivo Y,N,Y.

cells.label: Has a coat and a bag?
Has a coat or a hat (or both)?

questions.explanation: Count both the yes group and the no group, then keep the larger. Coat gives 5/4, hat 4/5, coat-and-bag 3/6, and coat-or-hat 7/2.

questions.prompt: What is the fewest yes/no questions that guarantees finding the right locker, if you may adapt each question to earlier answers?
questions.context: A prize is hidden in one of 11 numbered lockers. Each question may be any yes/no question about which lockers could hold it.
questions.explanation: Each answer can at best halve the candidates. Three questions separate at most 8 lockers, while four separate up to 16, so 11 needs four.

questions.prompt: You now learn the hidden item is red. Which question leaves the fewest possibilities in the worst case?
questions.context: Items (Color / Writes / Metal part / Moving part / Measures): Pen red,Y,Y,Y,N. Pencil red,Y,N,N,N. Ruler red,N,Y,N,Y. Stapler red,N,Y,Y,N. Eraser red,N,N,N,N. Scissors red,N,Y,Y,N. Tape blue,N,N,N,N. Glue blue,N,N,N,N.

options.label: Does it have a metal part?
Does it have a moving part?

questions.explanation: Among the six red items, moving part splits 3 and 3. Metal leaves up to 4, writing up to 4, and measuring up to 5.

questions.prompt: Order these questions from smallest to largest worst-case remaining group.
questions.context: A hidden card is numbered 1 to 12. Each question below gets a yes or no answer, and the order must rank them by the larger group they could leave.
questions.explanation: Worst cases are even 6, prime 7, at most 4 gives 8, multiple of 5 gives 10, and exactly 12 gives 11.

questions.prompt: Choose which investigation to follow next; both end with a hidden item found from supplied answers.
questions.context: The toolbox case uses four clues about hand tools. The parcel case uses three clues about packages. Either path takes one more task.
questions.explanation: Both cases use the same method: apply each supplied answer, cross out every candidate that conflicts, and stop when exactly one remains.

questions.prompt: Which tool is hidden, given all four answers?
questions.context: Traits (Powered / Cuts / Metal head / Turns): Hammer N,N,Y,N. Wrench N,N,Y,Y. Tape measure N,N,N,N. Pliers N,Y,Y,N. Level N,N,N,N. Saw N,Y,Y,N. Drill Y,N,Y,Y. Screwdriver N,N,Y,Y. Answers: Powered? No. Cuts? No. Metal head? Yes. Turns something? No.
questions.explanation: Powered-no removes Drill, cuts-no removes Pliers and Saw, metal-yes leaves Hammer, Wrench and Screwdriver, and turns-no leaves only Hammer.

questions.prompt: After each answer, how many parcels remain? Then name the hidden parcel.
questions.context: Traits (Heavy / Fragile / Red label): Alder Y,Y,N. Birch Y,N,Y. Cedar Y,Y,Y. Dune N,Y,N. Elm N,N,Y. Fern Y,N,N. Gale N,Y,Y. Haze Y,Y,N. Iris N,N,N. Answers in order: Heavy? Yes. Fragile? Yes. Red label? Yes.
questions.explanation: Heavy leaves Alder, Birch, Cedar, Fern and Haze. Fragile leaves Alder, Cedar and Haze. Only Cedar also has a red label.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All candidate lists, tool traits, parcels and cards are invented for this puzzle, and each case supplies every fact you need. The investigation choice is unscored, and the result counts only objective answers.

title: The Unreliable Lighthouse Log
description: Sort lighthouse log entries into true and false, match entries to the keepers who wrote them, then use liar-and-truth-teller clues to find the lamp's real state.

sections.title: Sort the entries
sections.description: Decide which log lines are true.

sections.title: Find the writers
sections.description: Link entries to keepers.

sections.title: Find the lamp
sections.description: Prove the lamp's true state.

questions.prompt: Mark each entry in Log 1 as true or false.
questions.context: Invented Log 1: the lamp was either on or off at midnight. Exactly one of the three entries is false.

left.label: Ada: The lamp was off at midnight.
Beck: The lamp was on at midnight.
Cora: The lamp was off at midnight.

questions.explanation: If the lamp were on, Ada's and Cora's entries would both be false, giving two falsehoods. So it was off, making only Beck's entry false.

questions.prompt: Mark each entry in Log 2 as true or false.
questions.context: Invented Log 2: exactly two of these four entries are false.

left.label: The supply boat arrived before noon.
The supply boat did not arrive before noon.
The boat arrived before noon and the dock light was on.

questions.explanation: The first two contradict, so exactly one is false. If the boat arrived, the last two would be both true or both false, never exactly one false. So it did not arrive, and the dock light was on.

questions.prompt: Match each entry to the keeper who wrote it.
questions.context: Invented facts: the lamp was lit, the door was locked, the bell was silent, and the wind came from the east. Iris wrote only true non-weather entries. Tomas wrote only false non-weather entries. Wen wrote every weather entry.

left.label: A west wind blew all night.

questions.explanation: Weather entries go to Wen, even a false one. Among the rest, true lines belong to Iris and false lines belong to Tomas, so keepers can own several entries.

questions.prompt: Match each tagged entry to the keeper who wrote it.
questions.context: Invented facts: the oil was low, the lens was clean, and the lamp was lit. Ada wrote only true dusk entries. Beck wrote only false dusk entries. Cora wrote every dawn entry.
questions.explanation: The dawn tag settles Cora's entries whatever their truth. For dusk lines, check each against the facts: true goes to Ada, false goes to Beck.

questions.prompt: What was the lamp's true state?
questions.context: Invented log: exactly one of three keepers lied, and the other two told the truth. Ada: "The lamp was off." Beck: "The lamp was on." Cora: "Beck is lying."
questions.explanation: If Ada lied, Beck would be truthful, making Cora a second liar. If Cora lied, Beck would be truthful and Ada would also lie. Only Beck lying works, so the lamp was off.

questions.prompt: Which option gives the lamp's true state and the keepers' types?
questions.context: Invented log: each keeper always tells the truth or always lies. Ada: "Beck is a liar." Beck: "Cora is a liar." Cora: "The lamp is off, and Ada is a liar."

options.label: Dark; Ada and Cora are truthful

questions.explanation: If Cora were truthful, Beck would be a liar and Ada truthful, contradicting her claim. So Cora lies, Beck is truthful, Ada lies, and Cora's claim fails only if the lamp is on.

questions.prompt: Classify each keeper as always truthful or always lying.
questions.context: Invented log: Dina says, "Emil and I are the same type." Emil says, "Fay is truthful." Fay says, "Dina is a liar."
questions.explanation: Whether Dina is truthful or lying, her claim forces Emil to be truthful. Then Fay is truthful, so Dina really is a liar, and every statement fits.

questions.prompt: Which option gives the lamp's state and the liars?
questions.context: Invented log: exactly two of four keepers lied. Hana: "The lamp is off." Ivo: "The lamp is on." Gus: "Ivo and Hana are both lying." Jun: "The lamp is off, or Gus is truthful."

options.label: Lit; Hana, Gus and Jun lie

questions.explanation: If the lamp were on, Hana, Gus and Jun would all lie, which is three liars. If it was off, Hana and Jun are truthful, while Ivo and Gus lie, exactly two.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All keepers, logs and lighthouse events are invented for this puzzle. Each task gives every rule you need, so no outside knowledge is required.

title: Fold, Punch, Unfold
description: Predict where holes land after a paper is folded and punched, then work backward from a hole pattern to the folds and punch spot that made it.

sections.title: Predict the holes
sections.description: Fold, punch, and picture the unfolded sheet.

sections.title: Work backward
sections.description: Use a finished pattern to choose the folds and punch.

questions.prompt: The top half is folded down over the bottom half, then a hole is punched in the packet's lower-left area. Tap the second hole after unfolding.
questions.context: The unfolded sheet is shown as four quadrants. The punch goes through both layers, away from the fold. The first hole is already in the lower-left quadrant.
questions.explanation: A fold across the middle mirrors the hole top-to-bottom. The lower-left hole gets a partner directly above it, in the upper-left quadrant, with the same left-right position.

diagram.title: Unfolded square sheet in four quadrants
diagram.description: A square sheet split into four equal quadrants with a horizontal midline and a vertical midline. Zones are labeled by their position on the unfolded sheet.

questions.prompt: Where is the partner hole after unfolding?
questions.context: A sheet has columns 1 to 4 from left to right and rows A to D from top to bottom. The left half is folded over the right half. A hole is punched at column 3, row B.
questions.explanation: The fold lies between columns 2 and 3, so columns 2 and 3 are mirror partners. Rows do not change, so the new hole is at column 2, row B.

questions.prompt: After unfolding, what does the sheet show?
questions.context: A sheet is folded once in half. A round punch is centered exactly on the folded edge, so it cuts through both layers.
questions.explanation: The punch is centered on the fold, so each layer holds half of the circle. Unfolded, the two halves join into one complete round hole on the crease.

options.label: Two separate round holes beside the crease
One complete round hole on the crease
Two half-circle notches on opposite edges

questions.prompt: Match each folding situation to the number of holes after unfolding.
questions.context: Every fold halves the packet, so the layers double. Each punch lands away from all folds and edges, and goes through every layer.
questions.explanation: Each halving fold doubles the layers: 1, 2, 4, then 8 layers. With the punch away from every fold, the hole count equals the layer count.

cells.label: Sheet laid flat, no folds, one punch
Folded in half once, one punch
Folded in half twice, one punch
Folded in half three times, one punch

questions.prompt: The unfolded sheet has holes only near its four outer corners. Which zone of the packet was punched?
questions.context: The left half was folded over the right half, then the top half was folded down over the bottom half. The packet is a quarter-size square drawn in the same orientation as the sheet, with the unmoved bottom-right layer underneath.
questions.explanation: The unmoved layer is the sheet's lower-right quadrant. Its lower-right corner is the sheet's own corner, and the folds mirror that hole into the other three corners.

diagram.title: Folded packet divided into four zones
diagram.description: A small square packet with four equal zones, shown in the same orientation as the original sheet. The punch happened in exactly one zone.

questions.prompt: Put the steps in order so the paper is folded, punched, and then fully unfolded.
questions.context: Two folds are made, then one punch. Unfold carefully so the last fold you made is the first one you undo.
questions.explanation: Folds are made first, then the punch, then they are undone in reverse. The top-over-bottom fold came last, so it opens first, and the left fold opens after it.

items.label: Punch one hole through the packet
Fold the left half over the right half
Fold the top half down over the bottom half

questions.prompt: The finished sheet has exactly two holes, at its upper-left and upper-right. Which fold-and-punch plan makes that?
questions.context: Each plan uses a single punch away from the folds. Plans describe the packet's position as it lies on the table.
questions.explanation: A left-right fold mirrors a hole across the vertical midline, giving a left and right pair in the same row. Punching the packet's upper area puts that pair at the top.

options.label: Fold the bottom half up over the top half; punch the packet's upper-right area
Fold left over right, then top over bottom; punch the packet's lower-right area
Fold the left half over the right half; punch the packet's upper-right area
Fold the left half over the right half; punch the packet's lower-right area

questions.prompt: After the diagonal fold, where is the partner of the punched hole once the sheet is unfolded?
questions.context: A sheet has columns 1 to 4 from left to right and rows 1 to 4 from top to bottom. It is folded along the diagonal from the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner. A hole is punched at column 4, row 2.
questions.explanation: A diagonal fold swaps the column and row numbers of a point. The hole at column 4, row 2 therefore has a partner at column 2, row 4.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All sheets, grids, and diagrams are original schematic drawings with text descriptions, so none depends on color. Folded layers are assumed to line up exactly.

title: Homophone Radio Relay
description: Work through a relay of sound-alike words: complete sentences with the right spelling, match words to sentences, then use an original tone cue to decide between two spellings that both fit.

questions.prompt: Clip transcript: 'The knight rode all ___.' Choose the spelling that completes the sentence.
questions.explanation: The sentence needs the time of darkness, spelled night. Knight sounds the same but names an armored rider, which would repeat the subject.

questions.prompt: Clip transcript: 'The baker will ___ the dough for ten minutes.' Which spelling fits?
questions.explanation: Knead means to press and fold dough. Need sounds identical but means to require something, so it does not describe working dough.

questions.prompt: Clip transcript: 'Please ___ the letter aloud before you sign it.' Pick the correct spelling.
questions.explanation: Read is the present-tense verb here, pronounced like reed. Red sounds like the past-tense read, but 'Please' calls for the present form.

questions.prompt: Clip transcript: 'I can't ___ the announcer over the noise.' Which spelling completes it?
questions.explanation: Hear is the verb for perceiving sound. Here means in this place, and heir names someone who inherits, so neither fits the sentence.

questions.prompt: Match each sentence gap to the spelling that fits. Some spellings are used more than once.
questions.explanation: There marks a place, their shows possession, and they're is short for 'they are'. Test by expanding: 'they are waiting' works, 'their waiting' does not.

left.label: The dogs wiped ___ paws on the mat.
The kids said ___ ready to go.

questions.prompt: Fill every gap with the correct spelling in this relay grid.
questions.explanation: Wrote is the past of write, right is the direction, two is the number, and weather describes sky conditions. Each has a sound-alike that changes the meaning.

cells.label: I ___ you a postcard last week.
The sun shone and the ___ was warm.

questions.prompt: Clip: 'Dana pointed at the ___.' Both sail and sale fit grammatically. Use the tone cue to choose.
questions.explanation: The rising two-tone cue means the cloth on a boat, so sail is correct. Without the cue, sale would also complete the sentence.
questions.context: Cue legend for this clip: a rising pair of tones (low then high) means the cloth on a boat. A falling pair (high then low) means a discount event at a shop.
questions.transcript: Two soft tones: a low 300 Hz tone, then a higher 600 Hz tone after a short pause, so the pitch rises.

questions.prompt: Clip: 'Omar pointed at the ___ on the shelf.' Flower and flour both fit. Use the tone cue to choose.
questions.explanation: Three short equal pulses mean a garden plant, so flower is correct. A single long low tone would have signalled the baking ingredient, flour.
questions.context: Cue legend for this clip: three short equal pulses mean a garden plant. One long low tone means a baking ingredient ground from grain.
questions.transcript: Three short, equal 500 Hz pulses, each a tenth of a second long, starting a quarter-second apart.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: This relay uses written transcripts and original tone cues instead of voice recordings. Sentences are invented for the quiz, and the cue legends are explained in each clip.

title: Mirror Sign Reader
description: Decode eight mirrored signs: recover true words from reflected letter order, correct flipped arrows, and rebuild a corridor of signs from its reflection.

questions.prompt: Which word is the sign's true reading?
questions.context: A left-right wall mirror shows a banner. Reading its letters from left to right in the reflection gives D-R-A-W-E-R, each letter itself flipped. A mirror reverses the order of letters.
questions.explanation: A left-right mirror reverses letter order, so D-R-A-W-E-R becomes R-E-W-A-R-D. The other options use the wrong order or different letters.

questions.prompt: What does the real sign say?
questions.context: In a left-right mirror, a shop sign appears with letters in this order from left to right: L-A-G-E-R. Every letter glyph is also flipped.
questions.explanation: Reverse the sequence L-A-G-E-R and you get R-E-G-A-L. LARGE and GLARE are anagrams, but the mirror reverses order rather than shuffling it.

questions.prompt: Choose the word that is actually printed on the station board.
questions.context: The reflection of a station board shows letters from left to right as S-M-A-R-T in a left-right mirror. The real board was printed in a plain sans-serif style.
questions.explanation: The true word is the reflection's letters read backward: T-R-A-M-S. TRAMP shares the first four letters but ends wrongly.

questions.prompt: Which longer word is on the real menu board?
questions.context: A left-right mirror shows a menu heading whose letters, left to right, are S-T-R-E-S-S-E-D. Letter shapes are flipped as well.
questions.explanation: Reversing S-T-R-E-S-S-E-D gives D-E-S-S-E-R-T-S. DESERTS is missing an S, and the other options keep the reflected order.

questions.prompt: Tap the panel showing the arrow's true direction.
questions.context: A wall mirror (a left-right flip) shows a direction arrow pointing up and to the right. The four panels show candidate real arrows.
questions.explanation: A left-right mirror swaps left and right but leaves up and down unchanged. An up-right arrow in the reflection is really pointing up-left.

diagram.title: Four candidate arrow directions
diagram.description: A 2 by 2 grid of panels. Each panel is labeled with the diagonal direction of the arrow it represents: top row points up, bottom row points down; left column points left, right column points right.

questions.prompt: Which way does the real arrow point?
questions.context: This time a polished floor acts as the mirror, flipping top to bottom while leaving left and right alone. The reflected arrow points up and to the right.
questions.explanation: A floor mirror swaps up and down but keeps left and right. A reflected up-right arrow is therefore a real down-right arrow.

questions.prompt: The real Library sign hangs at the far left of the corridor. Tap its slot in the mirror.
questions.context: The mirror shows the corridor wall as a left-right flip. The mirror image has three equal sign slots, from the viewer's left to right, and the Library sign is not yet drawn in.
questions.explanation: A left-right mirror swaps the two ends of the row. A sign at the real far-left slot appears in the right slot of the reflection.

diagram.title: Mirror row with three sign slots
diagram.description: A horizontal strip showing the reflection of a corridor wall, divided into three side-by-side empty slots labeled left, centre and right as seen in the mirror.

questions.prompt: Arrange the signs as they truly hang in the corridor, from far left to far right.
questions.context: In a left-right mirror, the reflected signs appear in this order from left to right: Café, Lift, Stairs, Exit. The real corridor is the reverse of that arrangement.
questions.explanation: A left-right mirror reverses the whole row. Reading the reflected order Café, Lift, Stairs, Exit backward gives Exit, Stairs, Lift, Café from left to right.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All signs, corridors and mirrors here are invented puzzle scenarios described in text, and the diagrams are simple schematic panels rather than photographs. Each puzzle states its mirror rule so you can solve it by reasoning.

title: Words Hiding Between Words
description: Scan short sentences, ignore the spaces, and find the word whose letters run across word boundaries. Hints start with a category and length, then fade to length only.

sections.title: Category Hints
sections.description: Each sentence hides one word of a stated length and type.

sections.title: Several at Once
sections.description: Match and fill in hidden words across multiple sentences.

sections.title: Length Only
sections.description: No category hint, just the word length.

questions.prompt: Which six-letter animal is hidden across the words of this sentence?
questions.context: Ignore spaces, punctuation and capitals. The hidden word's letters appear in order and cross at least one space. Sentence: "We watched a crab bite the rope."
questions.explanation: Reading "crab bite" without the space gives c-rabbit-e, so rabbit hides across the two words.

questions.prompt: Which six-letter fruit is hidden across words in this sentence?
questions.context: Sentence: "The actor angered the judge." Ignore spaces and capitals; the hidden word must cross at least one space.
questions.explanation: "Actor angered" runs together as act-orange-red, so orange is the fruit hiding across the two words.

questions.prompt: Which four-letter metal is hidden across words in this sentence?
questions.context: Sentence: "She found a big old coin in the attic." Ignore spaces; the answer crosses a word boundary.
questions.explanation: The words "big old" join to make bi-gold, so the metal is gold. None of the other metals appear in the sentence.

questions.prompt: Which five-letter musical instrument is hidden across words in this sentence?
questions.context: Sentence: "Urban joy filled the room." Ignore spaces and capitals; the hidden word crosses a word boundary.
questions.explanation: "Urban joy" becomes ur-banjo-y once the space is removed, so the instrument is the banjo.

questions.prompt: Match each sentence to the animal hiding across its words.
questions.context: Ignore spaces, punctuation and capitals. Each sentence hides exactly one of the four listed animals, and each animal is used once.
questions.explanation: The hiding places are wai-t-I-ger-ald (tiger), t-hors-e-emed (horse), su-e-a-gle-e-ful (eagle), and jessi-ca-mel-ted (camel).

left.label: Please wait, I, Gerald, will help.

questions.prompt: Choose the hidden word for each sentence, using the type and length given.
questions.context: Ignore spaces and capitals. Each hidden word crosses at least one word boundary.
questions.explanation: "Cup in kind" hides pink, "wolf our" hides four, and "Jo a kind" hides oak. The other options never appear across the spaces.

cells.label: Four-letter color in "Hold the cup in kind hands."
Four-letter number in "The wolf our group saw was shy."
Three-letter tree in "Ask Jo, a kind friend, to help."

questions.prompt: No category this time: which six-letter word is hidden across word boundaries, not inside a single word?
questions.context: Sentence: "Maria's plane tickets arrived." Ignore the apostrophe, spaces and capitals. Some options appear inside one word, so check where each one crosses a space.
questions.explanation: Ticket and arrive sit entirely inside single words. Planet is formed by the end of "plane" plus the start of "tickets".

questions.prompt: Find the six-letter word that starts in one word and ends in the next, with no category hint.
questions.context: Sentence: "Meg ardently studied maps." Ignore spaces and capitals. One option sits inside a single word, so it does not count.
questions.explanation: The last letter of "Meg" joins the start of "ardently" to spell garden. Ardent lies wholly inside "ardently", and gentle and studio never appear.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All sentences and names are invented for this quiz. Every answer can be found by removing spaces, and each is checked against the options shown.

title: Change One Letter, Fix the Sentence
description: Spot the one word in each nonsense sentence that a single swapped letter can repair, then choose the exact letter that makes the sentence sensible.

sections.title: Find the Broken Word
sections.description: Pick the one word to repair.

sections.title: Double Checks
sections.description: Two sentences at a time.

sections.title: Choose the Letter
sections.description: Name the replacement letter.

questions.prompt: Which word needs a one-letter change to make this sentence sensible?
questions.context: The chef served a bowl of hot soap.
questions.explanation: Changing the a in soap to u gives soup, which fits a served bowl. The other words already make sense.

questions.prompt: Which word is the one to fix by swapping a single letter?
questions.context: The farmer milked the cot before sunrise.
questions.explanation: Swapping the t in cot for w gives cow, the animal a farmer milks. Every other word already works.

questions.prompt: Which word should get a one-letter swap to repair the sentence?
questions.context: We rowed the boat across the lace to the island.
questions.explanation: Changing the c in lace to k gives lake, a body of water you can row across to reach an island.

questions.prompt: Which word needs one letter swapped so the sentence makes sense?
questions.context: The librarian stamped the date inside every hook.
questions.explanation: Changing the h in hook to b gives book, which is what a librarian stamps with a return date.

questions.prompt: For each sentence, choose the one word that needs a single-letter swap.
questions.explanation: Mutton becomes button with m to b, and beds becomes bees with d to e. Each repair restores a sensible, familiar scene.

cells.label: The tailor stitched a mutton onto my jacket.
The beds buzzed around the flowers in the garden.

questions.prompt: Again, pick the one word in each sentence to repair with a single-letter swap.
questions.explanation: Bell becomes ball with e to a, and gold becomes cold with g to c. Those swaps fit a goalkeeper and a chilly night.

cells.label: The goalkeeper caught the bell with both gloves.
Please close the window because the night air is gold.

questions.prompt: Which letter should replace the p in pain to repair the sentence?
questions.context: Take your umbrella; it looks like pain.
questions.explanation: Replacing p with r gives rain, which explains why you would take an umbrella. Main, tain and gain do not fit.

questions.prompt: Which letter should replace the u in bunch to repair the sentence?
questions.context: The tired runner finished the race, then sat down on a bunch.
questions.explanation: Replacing u with e gives bench, a seat for a tired runner. Banch, binch and bonch are not English words.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All sentences are invented for this quiz. A one-letter change means swapping one letter for another, never adding or removing letters.

title: Half-Clue Handoff
description: Two to four players take turns on one device, each answering every puzzle privately. Each puzzle's clues are split into a Player A half and a Player B half to share aloud, and the end screen compares everyone's actual answers.

sections.title: Split grids
sections.description: Each player has different rules.

questions.prompt: Combine both halves: which key is in each box?
questions.context: Keys: brass, silver, copper, one per box. Player A sees: brass is not in box 1; copper is not in box 2. Player B sees: silver is in box 2.
questions.explanation: Silver takes box 2. Brass cannot be in box 1, so brass is in box 3 and copper in box 1, which fits A's second rule.

questions.prompt: Pool your clues: which pet does each friend own?
questions.context: Asha, Bo and Chen each own a different pet: cat, dog or fish. Player A sees: Asha does not own the fish; Bo does not own the cat. Player B sees: Chen does not own the dog; Asha does not own the dog.
questions.explanation: Asha is neither fish nor dog, so she owns the cat. Chen cannot have the dog, so Chen has the fish and Bo the dog.

questions.prompt: Combine the halves: which day does each student present?
questions.context: Lucía, Kofi and Mei present on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday, one each. Player A sees: Kofi is not on Monday; Mei presents later than Lucía. Player B sees: Kofi is not on Wednesday.
questions.explanation: Kofi must be on Tuesday. That leaves Monday and Wednesday, and Mei is later than Lucía, so Lucía is Monday and Mei Wednesday.

questions.prompt: Agree on one order for setting up a classroom, first to last.
questions.context: Player A sees: the door is unlocked before anything else; the lights come on before the projector starts. Player B sees: worksheets are handed out after the lights are on; the projector starts before worksheets are handed out.
questions.explanation: The door comes first, then lights. The projector starts before worksheets, so the full chain is door, lights, projector, worksheets.

questions.prompt: Order the three houses from position 1 to position 3.
questions.context: Player A sees: red is not first; blue is not first. Player B sees: green is next to blue.
questions.explanation: Red and blue are not first, so green is first. Blue must be next to green, so blue is second and red third.

questions.prompt: Four market stalls stand in positions 1 to 4. Which stall is in position 2?
questions.context: Stalls: tea, bread, fruit, kites. Player A sees: fruit is at one end; tea is next to bread. Player B sees: kites is not at an end; bread is in position 4.
questions.explanation: Bread is 4, so tea is 3. Fruit must be at an end, so it takes position 1, leaving kites in position 2.

questions.prompt: Link each member to every room they could use, meaning at least one shared open day.
questions.context: Player A sees room days: Studio is open Mon and Wed; Lab is open Tue and Wed; Hall is open Mon and Tue. Player B sees member days: Pia is free Mon only; Quynh is free Tue and Wed; Rosa is free Wed only.
questions.explanation: Pia (Mon) fits Studio and Hall. Quynh (Tue, Wed) fits all three rooms. Rosa (Wed) fits Studio and Lab.

questions.prompt: Which three-digit lock code fits both halves of the clues?
questions.context: Digits come from 1 to 4, none repeated. Player A sees: the first digit is bigger than the second; the three digits add up to 7. Player B sees: the last digit is even and not 4.
questions.explanation: A digit sum of 7 means the digits are 1, 2 and 4. B puts 2 last, and A then forces 4 before 1, giving 412.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All puzzles are invented. Pass the device so that 2 to 4 players each submit private answers. The screen shows both clue halves, so for the handoff, Player A reads only A clues aloud and Player B only B clues; extra players join either side. Results show each player's accuracy and a side-by-side comparison of actual answers, not a measure of friendship or skill.

title: Hunch or Proof
description: Solve four small invented mysteries from complete clue sets, then answer four preference tasks about how many extra clues you like before naming a culprit and whether you build a story or run a checklist first. Your result shows accuracy from the mysteries and two preference scales, Answer-ready to Clue collector and Story-first to Checklist-first, separately.

sections.title: Solve the mysteries
sections.description: Every clue you need is on the page.

sections.title: Your clue appetite
sections.description: No right answers here, just a playful reveal style.

dimensions.description: How readily you name a culprit versus asking for one more clue first.
Whether you build a tale of the crime early or cross off suspects methodically.

questions.prompt: Who took the silver trophy from the club office?
questions.context: Invented case. Suspects: Ines, Omar, Priya, Tomas. Clue 1: the thief wore wet boots, and only Ines, Omar and Tomas had been outside in the rain. Clue 2: the thief knew the safe code, which only Omar and Priya knew.
questions.explanation: Wet boots leave Ines, Omar and Tomas. Knowing the safe code leaves Omar and Priya. Only Omar fits both clues.

questions.prompt: Put the night's café events in order using the notes.
questions.context: Invented case. Notes: the alarm was disabled before the delivery arrived. The register was opened after the delivery arrived. The missing cash was noticed after the register was opened.
questions.explanation: The notes form one chain: alarm, then delivery, then register, then discovery. Each event is fixed by the note linking it to its neighbour.

questions.prompt: Each guest was in a different room. Where was each one?
questions.context: Invented case. Rooms: Kitchen, Study, Garden, one guest each. Lena was not in the Kitchen. Kofi was not in the Study. Kofi was not in the Kitchen. Mei was not in the Garden.
questions.explanation: Kofi rules out Study and Kitchen, so he is in the Garden. Lena then has only the Study, leaving Mei in the Kitchen.

questions.prompt: Who knocked over the greenhouse plants?
questions.context: Invented case. Suspects: Dara, Elio, Faye, Gus. The plants were knocked over in the greenhouse during the afternoon. Clue 1: the culprit wore a red scarf, which Dara, Elio and Gus did. Clue 2: the culprit left before 4 pm, as did Elio, Faye and Gus. Clue 3: Gus was filmed at the front desk, away from the greenhouse, for the whole afternoon.
questions.explanation: Clues 1 and 2 leave Elio and Gus. Gus was away from the greenhouse all afternoon, when the plants fell, so Elio is the only suspect left.

questions.prompt: In a fresh mystery, how many extra clues do you usually want before naming someone?
questions.lowLabel: I'll answer on the first lead
questions.explanation: This is a style choice, not a skill measure. Neither end is better; it only sets your position on the descriptive clue-appetite scale.

questions.prompt: Rank these opening moves in a new mystery from most to least appealing.

items.label: Sketch a quick story of the crime, then test it
List every suspect and cross them off one by one
Ask for another clue before deciding anything
Name the likeliest suspect now and adjust later

questions.explanation: Your ordering shows which opening moves you enjoy. It is a playful preference, not a better or worse way to detect.

questions.prompt: Imagine a mystery game where an extra clue costs one point. Which approach would you choose?

options.label: Answer now after crossing off whoever I can
Pay the point, then reread all the clues as a checklist
Answer now once I can tell the story of the crime
Pay the point, then test the clue against my theory

questions.explanation: There is no correct choice here. Paying for evidence and answering early both suit different moods and puzzle rules.

questions.prompt: Match each puzzle setting to the approach you would most enjoy there.

left.label: A puzzle rewarding the fewest clues used

right.label: Answer from my story of the crime
Answer after a quick suspect checklist
Reveal a clue and rework my story
Reveal a clue and cross off suspects

questions.explanation: Your pairings show how the setting changes your style. Several settings can share one approach, and none is the right answer.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All mysteries are invented and every clue is shown on the page, so no extra clues are actually hidden. Your accuracy comes only from the four mysteries. The last four tasks place you on two descriptive scales, clue appetite and method; they are not a trait, ranking or measure of ability.

title: The Rule Sorting Machine
description: Send everyday words through three rule gates: starting letter, length, and a combined rule. Several words can land in the same bin.

questions.prompt: Send each word through the gate. Which bin receives it?
questions.context: Vowels are A, E, I, O, U only. Words starting with a vowel go to the Vowel bin. All other words go to the Consonant bin.
questions.explanation: Orange and umbrella start with O and U, so both share the Vowel bin. River starts with R and goes to the Consonant bin.

questions.prompt: How many of these words would the Vowel bin receive: ice, yellow, eagle, under, tree?
questions.context: Only A, E, I, O, U count as vowels. The letter Y does not count here.
questions.explanation: Ice, eagle and under start with I, E and U. Yellow starts with Y, which is not a vowel under this rule, and tree starts with T.

questions.prompt: Which list contains only words that the Vowel bin would accept?
questions.context: The gate checks only the first letter of each word. Vowels are A, E, I, O, U.
questions.explanation: Arrow, ivory, ember and uncle all begin with vowels. Each other list contains a word starting with Y, T or W.

questions.prompt: Count the letters, then send each word to its length bin.
questions.context: Short bin: 1 to 4 letters. Medium bin: 5 to 6 letters. Long bin: 7 or more letters.
questions.explanation: Lamp has 4 letters, river has 5, and garden has 6. River and garden therefore share the Medium bin.

questions.prompt: How many of these words reach the Long bin: bridge, lantern, notebook, window, sunshine?
questions.context: Long bin means 7 or more letters. Count each word carefully.
questions.explanation: Lantern has 7 letters, notebook has 8, and sunshine has 8. Bridge and window have only 6 each, so they stay out.

questions.prompt: Even-length words go to the Left bin and odd-length words go to the Right bin. Which word goes Right?
questions.explanation: Pencil, garden and window each have 6 letters, which is even. Lantern has 7 letters, which is odd, so it goes Right.

questions.prompt: Apply both rules in order, then place each word in its final bin.
questions.context: First, a word ending in A, E, I, O or U is Open; otherwise it is Closed. Then 5 or fewer letters is Low and 6 or more is Tall.
questions.explanation: Lake (4) and stone (5) end in E and are short, so they share Open and Low. Mountain ends in N and has 8 letters.

questions.prompt: How many of planet, harvest, cottage and plate land in the Closed and Tall bin?
questions.context: Open means the word ends in A, E, I, O or U; otherwise Closed. Tall means 6 or more letters.
questions.explanation: Planet (ends T, 6 letters) and harvest (ends T, 7) are Closed and Tall. Cottage ends in E, and plate ends in E with 5 letters.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All sorting rules are invented for this puzzle and stated in each task. Vowels are only A, E, I, O, U, and every rule works on spelling, not pronunciation.

title: Build Order: What Comes First?
description: Order fictional build tasks by their stated prerequisites, spot the step that breaks a plan, and add the missing step to finish it.

questions.prompt: Put the bookshelf tasks in an order that respects every prerequisite.
questions.context: Painting needs sanding finished. Sanding needs the frame built. Hanging the shelf needs the paint dry.
questions.explanation: Each rule links one task to the next, so the chain is forced: build, sand, paint, hang.

questions.prompt: Order the planter box tasks so no task starts before its prerequisites are done.
questions.context: Stapling the liner needs the box assembled. Adding soil needs the liner stapled. Painting the name label needs only the box assembled.
questions.explanation: Assembly comes first. Soil must follow the liner, while the label can go anywhere after assembly, so several orders are valid.

questions.prompt: Order the poster party tasks. Several valid orders exist, so follow the rules only.
questions.context: Cutting flyers needs them printed. Pinning flyers needs them cut and the board space booked. Booking the board needs nothing else.
questions.explanation: Printing leads to cutting, and both cutting and booking must finish before pinning. Booking can happen at any earlier point.

questions.prompt: Which step in this pottery plan is scheduled before its prerequisites are done?
questions.context: Plan: 1 Mix glaze, 2 Fire the cups, 3 Shape the cups, 4 Dip cups in glaze. Rules: dipping needs mixed glaze and shaped cups. Firing needs cups shaped and dipped.
questions.explanation: Firing at step 2 needs shaping and dipping, which come later. The other three steps have their prerequisites done by the time they run.

questions.prompt: Which step in this room plan runs before something it depends on?
questions.context: Plan: 1 Frame walls, 2 Wire, 3 Cover walls, 4 Insulate, 5 Lacquer floor. Rules: wiring needs framed walls. Insulating needs wiring. Covering walls needs insulation. Lacquer needs covered walls.
questions.explanation: Covering walls at step 3 needs insulation, which is not done until step 4. Insulating and lacquering both have their prerequisites finished in time.

questions.prompt: A delay in which task would delay every one of the other four tasks?
questions.context: Wiring needs the frame built. Windows need the frame built. Painting needs wiring and windows. Hanging lights needs painting.
questions.explanation: Wiring and windows both need the frame, and painting and lights follow from them. No other task is upstream of all four.

questions.prompt: This kite plan cannot work as written. Which missing step must be added?
questions.context: Plan: cut the sail, glue the sail on, attach the tail. Rules: gluing the sail needs a cut sail and a built cross frame. Attaching the tail needs the glued sail.
questions.explanation: Gluing needs a built cross frame, and the plan never builds one. The tail and sail steps are already present, and no rule requires the others.

questions.prompt: Order all five tasks, including the newly added dust-wiping step.
questions.context: Wiping dust needs sanding done. Staining needs the dust wiped. Sealing needs staining done. Cleaning brushes needs staining done.
questions.explanation: The chain sand, wipe, stain is forced. Sealing and brush cleaning both follow staining, in either order.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All projects and prerequisite rules are invented for this quiz. Every rule you need is stated in each task, and any order that satisfies the rules counts as correct.

title: Double Duty Words
description: Find the single word that completes two different sentences with two different meanings, sort word senses, and reject decoys that fit only one sentence.

questions.prompt: Which word completes both sentences?
questions.context: Sentence 1: "The ___ of the tree was rough." Sentence 2: "I heard the dog ___ all night."
questions.explanation: Bark is a tree's outer covering and also the sound a dog makes. Root, leaf and trunk suit only the tree sentence.

questions.prompt: Which word fits both the finger sentence and the arrival sentence?
questions.context: Sentence 1: "She wore a gold ___ on her finger." Sentence 2: "Please ___ me when you arrive."
questions.explanation: Ring is a circular piece of jewelry and also a verb meaning to telephone someone. Band and chain fit only the first; call fits only the second.

questions.prompt: Which word fits both the river sentence and the check sentence?
questions.context: Sentence 1: "We walked along the river ___." Sentence 2: "I need to ___ a check today."
questions.explanation: Bank is the land beside a river and also a verb meaning to deposit money. Shore and edge fit only the first; cash fits only the second.

questions.prompt: Which word fits both the pitch sentence and the cave sentence?
questions.context: Sentence 1: "The player swung the ___ at the pitch." Sentence 2: "A ___ flew out of the cave at dusk."
questions.explanation: A bat is both a club used in baseball and a flying mammal. The glove and ball do not fly out of caves, and an owl is not swung.

questions.prompt: For each pair of sentences, choose the single word that fits both.
questions.context: Pair A: "They will ___ a tree tomorrow." and "The ___ closes at five." Pair B: "Turn on the ___ to read." and "She packed a ___ bag for the trip."

cells.label: Pair A: tree / closes at five
Pair B: turn on / packed a bag

questions.explanation: Plant is a verb for putting in the ground and a noun for a factory. Light is a source of illumination and also means not heavy.

questions.prompt: Match each use of a double-duty word to the kind of meaning it carries.
questions.explanation: A dog's bark and ringing a bell are sounds or sound-making actions. Tree bark and a gold ring are physical things.

questions.prompt: Beware the decoy. Which word fits both sentences, not just one?
questions.context: Sentence 1: "Please ___ the letter." Sentence 2: "Put a ___ on the envelope."
questions.explanation: To stamp a letter means to mark it, and a stamp is also what you put on an envelope. Mail and send fit only the first; card fits only the second.

questions.prompt: Beware the decoy. Which word fits both the pouring sentence and the fastball sentence?
questions.context: Sentence 1: "She poured water from the ___." Sentence 2: "The ___ threw a fastball."
questions.explanation: A pitcher is a container for pouring and also the baseball player who throws pitches. Jug and glass fit only the first; umpire fits only the second.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All sentences are original, and each task supplies the sentences you need. Answers show both meanings of the bridging word.

title: Which Weighing Settles It?
description: Read balance-scale comparisons between abstract objects, find the heaviest, choose the one weighing that decides a puzzle, then order and classify claims from the chain.

questions.prompt: Using only these weighings, which item is the heaviest?
questions.context: Weighing 1: A is heavier than B. Weighing 2: B balances C exactly. Weighing 3: D is lighter than C.
questions.explanation: A is heavier than B, B equals C, and C is heavier than D. So A > B = C > D, which makes A the unique heaviest.

questions.prompt: Which shape is the heaviest according to these three weighings?
questions.context: Weighing 1: Cone is lighter than Disc. Weighing 2: Disc is lighter than Ring. Weighing 3: Cube balances Cone exactly.
questions.explanation: Cube equals Cone, Cone is lighter than Disc, and Disc is lighter than Ring. The chain Cube = Cone < Disc < Ring puts Ring on top.

questions.prompt: Which object is heaviest? Watch which side each object lands on.
questions.context: Weighing 1: Lamp is lighter than Mug. Weighing 2: Nail is heavier than Mug. Weighing 3: Kite balances Lamp exactly.
questions.explanation: Kite equals Lamp, Lamp is lighter than Mug, and Mug is lighter than Nail. So Kite = Lamp < Mug < Nail, and Nail is heaviest.

questions.prompt: Which objects are tied for the heaviest position?
questions.context: Weighing 1: Owl balances Pen exactly. Weighing 2: Pen is heavier than Quill. Weighing 3: Rope is lighter than Quill.
questions.explanation: Owl equals Pen, Pen beats Quill, and Quill beats Rope. So Owl = Pen > Quill > Rope, and the top spot is shared by Owl and Pen.

questions.prompt: You may add exactly one weighing. Which one is guaranteed to reveal the heaviest of the four?
questions.context: Known so far: B is heavier than A, and B is heavier than C. Nothing has been weighed against D yet.
questions.explanation: Only B or D can be heaviest, since A and C are already below B. Weighing B against D settles it either way. The other weighings can leave D untested against B.

questions.prompt: Which single extra weighing is guaranteed to decide the heaviest item?
questions.context: Known so far: Red is heavier than Blue. Green is heavier than Yellow. Blue balances Yellow exactly.
questions.explanation: Red beats Blue and Green beats Yellow, with Blue = Yellow, so the heaviest is Red or Green. Weighing Red against Green decides it. The other pairs are already implied.

questions.prompt: Arrange the four objects from lightest to heaviest using the weighings.
questions.context: Weighing 1: Fig is lighter than Gem. Weighing 2: Hat is lighter than Fig. Weighing 3: Gem is lighter than Ink.
questions.explanation: Hat is below Fig, Fig below Gem, and Gem below Ink. These three links form one chain, so exactly one order fits: Hat, Fig, Gem, Ink.

questions.prompt: For each claim, decide what the four weighings prove.
questions.context: Weighing 1: Pot is heavier than Cup. Weighing 2: Cup balances Dish exactly. Weighing 3: Spoon is lighter than Dish. Weighing 4: Tray is heavier than Spoon.
questions.explanation: Pot > Cup = Dish > Spoon, so Pot beats Spoon, and Spoon cannot beat Cup. Tray is only known to beat Spoon, so Tray versus Cup is open.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All objects and weighings are invented abstract puzzles. Each puzzle supplies every comparison you need, so no real-world weights or units are involved.

title: Guess the Gatekeeper's Rule
description: Study the words each gate lets through or turns away, name the hidden spelling rule, then predict which new words get accepted.

sections.title: Name the Rule
sections.description: Five gates, one fitting rule each.

sections.title: Next Word Through
sections.description: Use the pattern to predict new words.

questions.prompt: Which rule fits every accepted and rejected word at Gate 1?
questions.context: Gate 1 accepted: level, noon, kayak. Gate 1 rejected: house, tree. Exactly one option fits all five examples.

options.label: The word reads the same backward
The word has exactly five letters
The word contains two vowels side by side
The word starts with a consonant

questions.explanation: Palindromes: level, noon and kayak pass; house and tree fail. Five letters breaks on noon, vowel pairs break on level, and consonant starts break on house.

questions.prompt: Gate 2 uses a letter-order rule. Which rule matches all its examples?
questions.context: Gate 2 accepted: begin, ghost, almost. Gate 2 rejected: water, bring. Exactly one option fits all five examples.

options.label: Letters appear in alphabetical order from left to right
The word has six letters or fewer
The first letter is from A to M

questions.explanation: Alphabetical order lets begin, ghost and almost through, and stops water (w then a) and bring (r then i). The other rules wrongly accept or reject at least one example.

questions.prompt: What does Gate 3 look for in its words?
questions.context: Gate 3 accepted: balloon, coffee, tennis. Gate 3 rejected: planet, silver, garden. Exactly one option fits all six examples.

options.label: The same letter appears twice in a row
The word has more than five letters
The word contains the letter n
The word ends in a consonant

questions.explanation: Adjacent doubles: ll and oo in balloon, ff and ee in coffee, nn in tennis. Planet, silver and garden have none. Length, letter n and endings each fail somewhere.

questions.prompt: Which rule explains Gate 4's decisions?
questions.context: Gate 4 accepted: tent, nine, river. Gate 4 rejected: bird, melon. Exactly one option fits all five examples.

options.label: The first letter appears again later in the word
The word contains the letter e
The word has exactly one vowel
The word ends in a consonant

questions.explanation: Tent, nine and river repeat their first letter (t, n, r); bird and melon do not. Containing e fails on melon, one vowel on nine, consonant endings on nine.

questions.prompt: Which rule matches Gate 5 on a standard QWERTY keyboard?
questions.context: The top letter row is q w e r t y u i o p. Gate 5 accepted: tire, power, quiet. Gate 5 rejected: table, house. Exactly one option fits all five.

options.label: Every letter comes from the top keyboard row
The word contains the letter e
The word has five letters or fewer

questions.explanation: Top-row words: tire, power and quiet pass; table and house use other rows. Both rejected words contain e, have no repeats, and are five letters, so those rules fail.

questions.prompt: Gate 6 follows a first-and-last-letter rule. Which word will it accept next?
questions.context: Gate 6 accepted: alpha, stress, tenet. Gate 6 rejected: delta, garden. Only one candidate follows the pattern.
questions.explanation: The gate wants the same first and last letter: alpha, stress, tenet pass; delta and garden fail. Teapot starts and ends with t; mirror, planet and number do not.

questions.prompt: Which new word will Gate 7 accept?
questions.context: Gate 7 accepted: hijack, stone, defend. Gate 7 rejected: plum, window. Look at neighboring letters. Only one candidate matches the pattern.
questions.explanation: Gate 7 needs two neighboring letters that are consecutive in the alphabet, in order: hi, st, de. Cabin has ab. Mirror, plant and brown have no such pair; plum and window fail too.

questions.prompt: Decide whether Gate 8 will accept or reject each new word.
questions.context: Treat y as a consonant. Gate 8 accepted: plane, sunset, friend. Gate 8 rejected: idea, crypt. Apply the same pattern to each new word.
questions.explanation: Gate 8 accepts words with exactly two vowels: plane, sunset, friend, garden, stripe. It rejects idea and banana (three vowels) and crypt and rhythm (none).

title: Read the Fine Print Conditionals
description: Sort situations against everyday notices, then check what 'if', 'only if' and 'unless' rules do and do not establish, and rewrite them as plain rules.

sections.title: Sort the situations
sections.description: Match each situation to its verdict.

sections.title: Implication checks
sections.description: Decide what a rule proves.

sections.title: Plain rules
sections.description: Restate the fine print.

questions.prompt: Notice: 'Pets allowed only if registered.' Match each situation to its verdict.
questions.context: Breaks the rule: the stated outcome contradicts the notice. Fits the rule: the outcome is stated and agrees with the notice. Can't settle it: the outcome is not stated, and the notice alone does not decide it.
questions.explanation: 'Only if' makes registration necessary: an allowed pet must be registered. An unregistered pet that is approved breaks it. A registered pet with no stated outcome is not decided by the notice, since registration is not a guarantee.

left.label: An unregistered pet is approved to stay
A registered pet is approved to stay
A pet is registered; nothing is known about approval
An unregistered pet is turned away

questions.prompt: Notice: 'Guests may use the roof deck if accompanied by a resident.' Match each situation to its verdict.
questions.context: Breaks the rule: the stated outcome contradicts the notice. Fits the rule: the outcome is stated and agrees with the notice. Can't settle it: the outcome is not stated, and the notice alone does not decide it.
questions.explanation: Here 'if' gives a sufficient condition: accompaniment guarantees access. Refusing an accompanied guest breaks it. The notice says nothing about a guest who is alone, so refusing one fits, and an unstated outcome can't be settled.

left.label: A guest with a resident is refused entry
A guest with a resident is admitted
A guest arrives alone; nothing is known about access
A guest arrives alone and is refused

questions.prompt: Notice: 'Library fines are waived unless the book is returned late.' Match each situation to its verdict.
questions.context: Read 'unless' as 'if not': if the book is not late, the fine is waived. Breaks the rule: the stated outcome contradicts the notice. Fits the rule: the outcome is stated and agrees with the notice. Can't settle it: the outcome is not stated, and the notice alone does not decide it.
questions.explanation: The notice guarantees a waiver for on-time returns, so charging one breaks it. For late returns it promises nothing, so a stated charge fits, and an unstated outcome can't be settled.

left.label: An on-time book is charged a fine
An on-time book has its fine waived
A book is late; nothing is known about the fine
A late book is charged a fine

questions.prompt: Notice: 'Bikes may be stored in the cellar only if tagged.' Mia's bike is tagged. What follows?
questions.explanation: A tag is necessary, not sufficient. Tagging meets one requirement, but the notice does not rule out other conditions, so storage is not yet proven.

options.label: Her bike must be allowed in the cellar
The notice alone doesn't settle whether it is allowed
Untagged bikes must also be allowed

questions.prompt: Notice: 'Staff may enter the lab only if they have completed training.' Sam, a staff member, was admitted. Which must be true?
questions.explanation: Admission requires training, so an admitted person must have completed it. The notice does not say whether any further safety test exists or whether anyone else entered.

options.label: Sam completed training and passed a separate safety test
Everyone trained is allowed into the lab
Sam is the only person admitted

questions.prompt: Notice: 'The pool opens unless it is raining.' The pool is closed today and the notice was followed. What follows?
questions.context: Read 'unless' as 'if not': if it is not raining, the pool opens.
questions.explanation: If no rain guaranteed opening, a closed pool means that guarantee was not triggered. So it must be raining. The notice names no other reasons for closure.

options.label: Nothing can be concluded about the weather

questions.prompt: Notice: 'The discount applies only if you are a member.' Which conclusion does NOT follow?
questions.explanation: Membership is required for the discount, not a guarantee of it. Treating 'only if' as 'if and only if' wrongly promises the discount to every member.

options.label: A non-member does not get the discount
Anyone who got the discount is a member
Membership is necessary for the discount

questions.prompt: Choose the plain 'if A, then B' rewrite for each notice.
questions.explanation: 'Only if' flips the direction: allowed implies registered. Plain 'if' points forward from the condition, and 'unless' becomes 'if not' for the exception.

cells.label: Guests may enter if they have a pass

options.label: If entered, then no pass needed
If no pass, then not allowed

cells.label: Fines waived unless the book is late

options.label: If not waived, then not late

title: Shift Note Decoder
description: Decode short letter-shift notes in both directions, including wrap-around from Z to A, then use decoded words to solve small clues.

sections.title: Single Notes
sections.description: Apply the stated shift to one note.

sections.title: Decoding Tables
sections.description: Decode several notes at once.

sections.title: Clue Notes
sections.description: Decode two notes, then answer the clue.

questions.prompt: Which word was sent in this note?
questions.context: Decoding rule: shift each letter back by one (B becomes A, C becomes B). Note: DBU.
questions.explanation: D→C, B→A, U→T gives CAT. BAT would have been sent as CBU, and CAR as DBS.

questions.prompt: Which word does the note RKG stand for?
questions.context: Decoding rule: shift each letter back by two (C becomes A, D becomes B). Note: RKG.
questions.explanation: R→P, K→I, G→E gives PIE. PIG would have been sent as RKI, and TIE as VKG.

questions.prompt: Which word does the note PRK stand for?
questions.context: Decoding rule: shift each letter forward by three (P becomes S, R becomes U). Note: PRK.
questions.explanation: P→S, R→U, K→N gives SUN. Shifting the wrong direction would give nonsense, so the stated direction matters.

questions.prompt: The alphabet wraps around, so A follows Z. Which word was sent?
questions.context: Decoding rule: shift each letter back by one (A wraps back to Z). Note: APP.
questions.explanation: A→Z, P→O, P→O gives ZOO. APP is only the raw note, not the decoded word, and ZAP would have been sent as ABQ.

questions.prompt: Shift every note back by one. Match each note to its decoded word.
questions.context: One word on the right is not used by any note.
questions.explanation: IPU→HOT, DPME→COLD, XBSN→WARM. Each letter moves back one place; WET is a leftover that no note produces.

questions.prompt: Decode each note using its own stated shift and pick the word for every cell.
questions.explanation: JCV back two is HAT. AZC forward one is BAD, with Z wrapping around to A. WLQ back three is TIN. Direction and size both change per note.

questions.prompt: Decode both notes, then add the two locker numbers. What is the total?
questions.context: Invented locker chart: CAT = 12, DOG = 25, OWL = 31, BAT = 40. Shift every letter back by one. Note 1: EPH. Note 2: PXM.
questions.explanation: EPH decodes to DOG (25) and PXM decodes to OWL (31). The sum is 56.

questions.prompt: A pass lasts two of note 1's unit and counts in note 2's unit. How many units is that?
questions.context: Shift every letter forward by two to decode. Note 1: UCCI. Note 2: BYW. Use 1 week = 7 days.
questions.explanation: UCCI decodes to WEEK and BYW decodes to DAY. Two weeks is 2 × 7 = 14 days.
